With a live-rule cap of 8: wrong answers 0.556 vs 0.333 per world (difference -0.222 [-0.687, +0.243], lower in 1 of 9 worlds), one retirement. Budget 6000, no cap: 0.444 vs 0.444, reward 3.709 vs 3.707.

Wide drift (four families with plain rules change at half the budget; measurement-only world option), budget 3000, 11 of 20 worlds with a stale rule live, no cap:

| measure | no pruning | pruning |
|---|---|---|
| wrong answers produced by a rule, per world | 2.455 | 1.182 (difference -1.273 [-3.937, +1.391]; lower in 1 of 11 worlds) |
| share of rule answers that are wrong (pooled) | 0.500 | 0.361 |
| reward per energy | 3.667 | 3.668 (+0.002 [-0.002, +0.005]) |

Retirements in the pruning arm: 4 (3 low success, 1 merged), in 1 world with a retirement after the change (first one 47 steps after the change). **Wrong-rule use falls in the wide scenario, but the effect rests on one world and its interval includes zero; there is no reward effect.** Stationary control (no drift): reward identical with and without pruning (3.654); 2 merges in 20 worlds, no low-success retirement, so pruning did not remove good rules here.

Rule count over time (mean live rules over 20 worlds, no cap, narrow scenario, no pruning vs pruning): after step 25: 0.40 / 0.40, 100: 1.00 / 1.00, 200: 2.25 / 2.25, 300: 3.35 / 3.30, 400: 3.85 / 3.75, 600: 4.00 / 3.90 (wide: 3.70 / 3.55 at 400). Without a cap the largest rule count in any world was 15 (narrow, no pruning) and 13 with pruning; with a cap of 8 the largest was 8, with 6 cap refusals logged per arm.

### Caps and kill switch

Caps run (budget 3000, 20 worlds, composition on): live rules 3, building blocks 2, search candidates per pass 60, steps per run 400, energy per run 900. Largest value seen: live rules 3, blocks used 2, candidates per pass 60, steps 400: **no cap exceeded**. Energy: the cap stops new steps once reached; overshoot was at most 4 units (a step that starts below the cap may end above it). 19 of 20 runs ended at the energy cap, 1 at the step limit. Refusals recorded: search candidates 47, live rules 3, building blocks 4; in a logged run each is a `controller_refusal` event (tests compare counts with the log).

Kill switch: a check turned on before step 41 stopped 20 of 20 runs after exactly 40 steps. Tests also cover a KILL file present at the start (refused and audited), a KILL file created while the loop runs (the next check stops it: 7 steps ran, the file appeared at the 8th check) and the stop event in the log.

### What is tested (not measured)

controller.txt parsing (defaults, hard maxima, unknown or repeated keys, fail closed: every cap 0), the reserved-file refusal for every spelling of `controller.txt`, audit rows for each refusal kind, replay of composed and retired rules from the log alone (rule re-derivation includes composed rules), time travel across a retirement, nothing deleted, a capped search being a prefix of the uncapped search, the source scans (the being sources have no file or network API; `discover.rs` names no hidden family).

### What B5 does not show

No reward gain from composition; the pruning effect is small and rests on a few worlds; the families, transforms and rewards are the author's; the tuning grid was cut short; no real data, no real language model, no long unattended run, no crash recovery; sensitivity to the world design (the number of families sharing a signature, prefix length) was not swept.

## Track B6: transfer between domains (synthetic world, author-defined families)

Everything here is a simulation written by one author: the two phases of the world, the hidden value map, the families, the rewards, the solvers and the learner. "Transfer" means two specific things: (1) the cells of a new domain start from the posterior of the same (difficulty, strategy) cell of a learned domain, chosen by a similarity read from logged outcomes, with a guard that can switch the link off; (2) the rule search tries rules already accepted in the other domain first. Measured with `cargo run -p kore-self --example measure_being --offline --release -- b6` (also `b6 6000`, `b6-tune`, `b6-tune-guard`), 2026-10-31, branch self-b6 (built on self-b5 a79f7f31). Report seeds 1..20, tuning seeds 101..120 (used only for the settings below). Budgets 3000 (main) and 6000. Discovery pass every 10 steps, composition on, B5 learner (beta 1.5) in every arm.

World (`transfer: true`, needs extended2, default off; a test shows every earlier result is bit for bit unchanged). A life has two phases. Phase 1 (about the first 40% of the budget, moved by +-3% by the world seed, hidden) offers only sequence tasks, domain A (the extended2 families). From then on the offers are drawn from three domains: A again, B (`pattern_b`: the same families, but every term and the revealed next term are passed through a hidden affine map a*v+b with a in {2,3}, b in 1..9) and a control domain C (unit conversions, no sequence structure). B shares building blocks with A and is not identical: polynomial forms carry over unchanged, but recurrences without a constant term (geometric, Fibonacci-like, tribonacci-like) need a constant term in B, and the fixed solvers that were exact on A for geometric and Fibonacci-like sequences are no longer exact on B. B and A pay like each other (copied hidden profile, 2x pattern bonus); C pays like the units domain. B's rules are their own (signature = difficulty + 10), found on B's own revealed examples.

Mechanism (log-derived only, replay-exact). Similarity (`being/transfer.rs`): for the logged examples of B, the share on which the first applicable rule of A at the same difficulty (accepted in A after the full B2/B5 verification), or the same rule with its constant term toggled, gives the exact next term, pooled over difficulties; a link needs at least 3 examples, at least 2 right, no wrong application and a share of at least tau. Then every difficulty at which A's cell holds at least 4 effective attempts is linked. A linked cell takes the source cell's posterior as its prior (weight XFER_K pseudo-observations) in place of the strategy-wide chain; the `discovered` strategy of B is linked only once B has a live rule at that difficulty. Guard (`model.rs`): after at least 4 attempts a link influenced, if the observed outcomes are less likely under the transferred prior than under the plain prior by more than 2 nats of log-likelihood, the link is switched off for good. Every link and every revocation is a note plus a revision of `being/transfer/NNNN` citing the logged examples or attempts it rests on; links are read back from the log on replay, revocations are re-derived by the fold; a test checks that the replayed model equals the live one. The rule search under transfer: A's accepted rules (and constant-toggled forms) are tried first for the same difficulty in B; acceptance is unchanged (3 training and 1 held-out new exact reproductions, 3 spare equations, never applicable-and-wrong), so only the order of trial changes.

Settings, chosen on tuning seeds 101..120 only. tau 0.34 / 0.5 / 0.67 with XFER_K 4 / 8 / 16 (transfer minus no transfer, first 100 steps after B appears, reward per energy): tau 0.34: +0.183, +0.202, +0.215; tau 0.5: +0.181, +0.199, +0.213; tau 0.67: +0.050, +0.050, +0.053 (the 0.67 rows link in fewer worlds; the 0.34 and 0.5 rows differ by less than 0.005 and every interval overlaps). Chosen: tau 0.5, XFER_K 16. Guard threshold 0.5 / 1 / 2 / 3 / 5 nats (shifted-cells control, guard on minus guard off, first 100 steps): +0.235, +0.235, +0.232, +0.221, +0.199, all with 9 or 10 wins and 0 losses of 20; the right-source links the guard wrongly revoked per world: 0.15, 0.15, 0.00, 0.00, 0.00. Chosen: 2 nats (no false revocation on the tuning seeds, almost the same protection). The planned discovery-order switch was not tuned (it has no setting).

Arms on identical worlds (same world seed, same tasks): no transfer (the B5 learner); transfer (links, guard, search order); links only (transfer without the changed search order); three controls that use the same trigger as the transfer arm but the wrong source: "right domain, shifted cells" (the sequence domain A is the right source, but each difficulty borrows the cell of the next difficulty, cyclic), guard on and off, and "wrong similarity" (B linked to the most dissimilar learned domain other than A, C linked to the most dissimilar learned domain, by distance between pooled success rates of the fixed strategies), guard on and off; and an oracle (knows the hidden success rates, holds rules found with 150 examples per domain and difficulty). The controls exist to show what bad transfer would cost; the tools cannot switch them on.

### Budget 6000 (same worlds' seeds, schedule scaled with the budget, n = 20)

Reward per energy over the first 100 steps after B appears: no transfer 3.032 [2.637, 3.427], transfer 3.270 [2.743, 3.796], shifted cells guard on 2.829, guard off 2.542, oracle 4.379. Transfer minus no transfer: +0.281 [+0.068, +0.494] (9/0/11) over the first 50 steps, +0.237 [+0.080, +0.395] (11/0/9) over 100, +0.184 [+0.069, +0.299] (12/0/8) over 200, +0.041 [+0.019, +0.063] (11/1/8) over the whole time after. Shifted cells (guard on) minus no transfer: -0.203 [-0.385, -0.020] (1/10/9) over 100 steps; guard off -0.490 over 100 steps (3.032 against 2.542). Wrong similarity guard on minus off: +0.001 [-0.001, +0.004] over 100 steps. Worlds reaching 90% of the oracle's B rate: no transfer 6 of 20 (median 138 steps), transfer 8 of 20 (64 steps), oracle 20 of 20 (69). Rules: 0 applicable-and-wrong in every arm; one rule per arm (the same world, id+lin.1 at difficulty 4 of A) was never applicable on 300 fresh tasks (it was accepted on a coincidence of its examples, never applicable-and-wrong, and it is also in the no-transfer arm, so transfer did not cause it).

### Verdict

* Transfer gives a modest, repeatable gain early: +0.21 reward per energy over the first 100 steps after B appears (95% interval +0.05 to +0.37, better in 11 of 20 worlds, worse in 0, 9 ties), about a 7% gain on a base of 2.82 and about 13% of the gap to the oracle (regret 1.58 to 1.37). The gain shrinks with time (+0.10 over the whole time after at budget 3000, +0.04 at 6000) because the no-transfer learner catches up. It does not reach the oracle, which stays about 1.4 better early on.
* Reaching 90% of the oracle's rate on B: 8 of 20 worlds against 6, and 45 steps earlier at the median (78 against 123), with the paired comparison resting on 6 worlds.
* Negative transfer is real in this design and the guard helps. Borrowing the wrong cells of the right domain costs -0.20 [-0.36, -0.04] over 100 steps (worse in 9 of 20 worlds, better in 2) with the guard on and -0.39 [-0.64, -0.14] (worse in 11, better in 0) with the guard off; the guard recovers +0.18 [+0.06, +0.31] (10 wins, 0 losses) and revoked 19 of 59 links, but it does not remove the harm. The real similarity trigger produced 1 revocation and no loss in 20 worlds.
* The wrong-similarity control (links to the most dissimilar learned domain) shows no significant cost or guard effect: it linked B in only 5 cases, because the dissimilar domain C is often not learned enough to lend anything, and it linked C in 6 worlds with a non-significant loss on C (-15.5 points, interval -38.5 to +7.6). It does not show that dissimilar-domain transfer is harmless; it shows that it rarely happened.
* The changed order of the rule search has no effect at all (20 ties of 20 on every window), as expected for an order change under unchanged acceptance rules. All the benefit comes from the links.
* Wrong rules accepted: 0 applicable-and-wrong in every arm and budget (one inert rule per arm at budget 6000, in the no-transfer arm too).

### What B6 does not show

The gain is small, concentrated in 11 or 12 of 20 worlds, and the interval for the whole time after B is narrow only because most of the run is shared by the arms. The link raises the estimated value of B early; the shifted-cells control separates the right cells from wrong ones, but there is no control that gives B a generic optimism bonus unrelated to any source, so part of the gain may be early exploration of B and not specific knowledge. No rule is transferred directly: B's rules still need B's own examples under the unchanged evidence bar, and rule discovery did not get faster per example (only earlier in time, because B was attempted earlier). The transformation (an affine map), the families, the 40% schedule, the similarity (rule-fit on one source domain, only A can be a source for B), the 0.5/16/2 settings, the control domain and the rewards are all the author's; B has a single source domain, so "most similar learned cell" is a choice among one real candidate; the wrong-similarity control rarely fired; the tuning grid was small (9 + 5 settings); the oracle's rule book comes from 150 sampled examples per signature, not from the author's knowledge of the families; no real data, no real language model, no long unattended run, no crash recovery; sensitivity to the world design (the map, the number of families sharing a signature, the phase length) was not swept.

### What is tested (not measured)

Earlier results bit for bit unchanged with the option off (golden digests recorded with the B5 code, plus no new domain ever offered); the two phases and the hidden affine map of the world; the transferred search order keeps the full verification (every rule found is never applicable-and-wrong on all examples of its signature, with the same minimum support; no preference means exactly the composed search; a hypothesis that is not a candidate is ignored); the guard revokes a harmful link, keeps a good one, does nothing with the guard off and lends nothing from a source with too little evidence; links are logged as notes and revisions that cite the logged examples, replay gives the same model, links and rules, and the log before the first link note has no link; transfer is off unless the being was created with it; `controller.txt` keys `transfer` (default off) and `max_transfer_links` (default 16, hard maximum 1000, unparseable values fail closed); a cap on links is a logged refusal and the live number never exceeds it; a controller that does not allow transfer refuses it once, logs it and audits it (tool level as well); no wrong rule accepted in the transfer and control arms; the measurement is deterministic; the transfer and model sources name no hidden world parameter and use no file or network API.

## World v2: the existing learner in a larger world (synthetic world, author-defined families)

Design: `docs/world_v2.md`. Everything is a simulation written by one author: 5 family types (hidden-rule sequences with 12 rule classes, grid shortest paths with a hidden move rule, knapsacks, formulas with a hidden constant g, compositional sequence tasks that reuse another family's rule), feedback noise (the being is told the wrong verdict at a hidden per-family rate) and hidden drift (a family's whole regime is re-drawn at seeded times). The learner is the EXISTING one, not a new one: the B1 model and planner keyed by family (a test checks bit-for-bit equality with `model.rs` and 1500 identical decisions with `planner.rs`) plus the B2 rule search every 10 steps. Score: the TRUE reward per energy unit (the checker's verdict), not the reward the being was told. Measured with `cargo run -p kore-self --example measure_world_v2 --offline --release -- report` (and `-- tune`), 2026-11-05, branch `world-v2` on c7e5d8c3. Report seeds 1..20, tuning seeds 101..120. Intervals: 95% t-interval of the mean over the 20 worlds; paired differences on identical worlds.

Tuning (seeds 101..120, 12 families, budget 3000, noise 50, drift 10): learner beta 0.5 / 1 / 1.5 / 2 / 3: 2.616, 2.745, 2.896, 2.863, 2.816 (intervals overlap); UCB1 c 0.02 / 0.05 / 0.2 / 0.5 / 1: 2.055, 2.113, 1.693, 1.124, 0.862. The existing defaults (beta 1.5, c 0.05) scored best and are used.

Conditions: small = 6 families, budget 1500; medium = 12 families, budget 3000; large = 24 families, budget 6000. clean = no noise, no drift, flat difficulty; noisy = noise 100 per mille (family rates 0, 10% or 20%); drift = 20 changes per 10 000 energy; hard = noise 100, drift 20 and a rising difficulty curve (100%). Policies: random; always-fast / careful / deep (best listed reward per listed cost); UCB1 over (family, strategy) arms; learner without discovery; learner; oracle-planner (knows the true success rate of every fixed strategy per (family, difficulty) in the current regime); oracle-knows-rules (may also answer with the checker's own answer at the listed energy, careful slips). Both oracles skip with the learner's skip rule on their expected rate; they are strong references, not proven optima (in 2 to 6 of 20 worlds the learner beats an oracle).

The caps never bound and composition changed no decision. Baselines that do not learn, and the oracles, do not see the noise, so their clean and noisy columns are the same numbers.

### Where the existing learner fails (the main result)

1. **It barely uses what it discovers, and in the large world not at all.** Discovery minus no discovery: +0.044 [-0.026, +0.114] (small), +0.024 [-0.006, +0.055] (medium), -0.000 (large clean), -0.005 [-0.015, +0.004] (large hard); not significant anywhere, 14 to 19 ties of 20. Rules were accepted (2.2, 3.9 and 5.2 per world in small, medium and large clean; 0 wrong on fresh tasks at acceptance; 0 below 90% right at the end of the life), but in the large clean world the learner tried the `discovered` strategy 84 times in 20 lives and answered **0** tasks with a rule (104 rules accepted). In medium clean, 572 of 3510 sequence/compose attempts used a rule (522 right). Cause, from the design of the B1 planner: a new rule only resets the (family, difficulty, discovered) cell to its prior; nothing tells the planner that a rule now applies, and with 24 families x 5 difficulties x 4 strategies the optimism bonus of one such cell rarely beats well-estimated cells.
2. **Most of the gap to the oracles is in the sequence, compose and formula families.** Medium clean, true reward per energy where the energy was spent (learner vs oracle-knows-rules): seq 2.86 vs 4.27, compose 2.49 vs 3.82, formula 2.22 vs 3.62, grid 3.74 vs 4.85, knap 2.95 vs 3.97. Formula families whose hidden g differs from the textbook 10 cannot be solved by any strategy the being has, and the learner keeps spending on them: 14% (large clean) to 76% (small clean) of its formula energy went to such families, earning 0.000 to 0.026 per energy. The existing learner has no way to fit a constant across tasks although every revealed answer is in its log.
3. **Hidden move rules of grid families are only partly learned:** 56% (medium clean) to 84% (large hard) of grid energy went to a strategy other than the breadth-first search that matches the hidden move rule (the Manhattan heuristic is often right on 4-neighbour grids, so not all of this is loss); the learner's grid rate is 3.7 to 4.2 against 4.8 to 5.1 for the oracles.
4. **Slow start.** Learner as a share of oracle-knows-rules over the first quarter of the energy: 0.653 [0.535, 0.771] small, 0.681 [0.584, 0.779] medium, 0.624 [0.532, 0.717] medium noisy, 0.619 [0.530, 0.707] medium hard, 0.760 [0.665, 0.854] large clean (twice the budget per quarter); over the last quarter 0.83 to 0.89. Whole-life share: 0.774 [0.682, 0.866] small, 0.800 [0.707, 0.894] medium, 0.859 [0.773, 0.945] large (clean).
5. **Feedback noise silences discovery.** With noise, rules per world fall from 3.9 to 2.7 (medium) and to 1.8 (medium hard), and rule-answered attempts from 572 to 312 and 161: one wrong revealed answer makes a correct rule "applicable and wrong" on its examples and the B2 guard then rejects it for good. No wrong rule was accepted under noise (0 of 54, 0 of 36, 0 of 92). The planner's beliefs carry the noise: mean predicted success 0.741, reported 0.715, true 0.762 (medium noisy). The total cost of noise to the learner is small (2.755 to 2.713 on medium, intervals overlap) because most of its reward comes from families that need no rule.
6. **Drift and rising difficulty widen the gap.** oracle-planner minus learner: +0.476 [+0.235, +0.718] (medium clean, 18/2/0), +0.581 [+0.314, +0.849] (drift, 20/0/0), +0.671 [+0.370, +0.973] (hard, 20/0/0); oracle-knows-rules minus learner +0.634 clean against +0.823 hard. The B1 learner never forgets, so a changed regime is learned only as fast as new evidence outweighs old.

What it does well: it beats every baseline in every condition: random by about +2.0 (20 of 20), the best fixed strategy of each world chosen in hindsight by +1.19 to +1.44 (19 or 20 of 20) and UCB1 over (family, strategy) arms by +0.49 [+0.11, +0.87] to +0.69 [+0.40, +0.99] (13 to 18 of 20); it reaches 77% to 86% of oracle-knows-rules and 80% to 90% of oracle-planner. Most of this comes from choosing family and strategy per cell and from skipping menus (6% to 13% of its energy goes to skips), the same levers as in B1, not from learning hidden rules.

### What is tested (not measured)

Determinism (two logged runs write identical logs; the logged run equals the unlogged measurement step for step); replay from the log alone (state folded from the log equals the live state; every learner decision and every rule re-derived, also after a continued run); every decision revision cites the genesis event and existing outcome events; checkers against independent statements of every hidden rule (BFS; knapsack against brute force; formula with the hidden g; every sequence class generator follows its rule); the fixed solvers cover exactly the classes the design says, and the B2 grammar accepts every in-grammar class and neither negative control; feedback noise has the configured rate and is self-consistent; drift happens on schedule only; config validation (a refused request writes nothing); bit-for-bit equivalence with the B1 model and decision equivalence with the B1 planner; controller caps (live rules, search candidates, energy, steps) hold and refusals are logged; the kill switch stops the run before any further step and is logged; tool level: missing `controller.txt` refused and audited, `world_v2_run` denied by `authorize()` unless listed under [L2], KILL file refused and audited, KILL appearing mid-run stops the run, the controller's energy cap stops it; a World v2 being in the same log leaves the original being's rows, state and replay identical; the World v2 sources use no file, network or process API, and the learner's files name no hidden parameter.

### What World v2 does not show

All families, rules, noise, drift and rewards are the author's, and so is the learner; the B2 grammar covers 10 of the 12 sequence classes by construction; noise is independent per attempt; drift re-draws a whole regime at once; grid and knapsack have nothing to learn beyond strategy choice; the oracles are references, not optima; 20 worlds per condition, one budget per size; no real data, no language model, no long unattended run.

## Track B3b: adaptation, second attempt (synthetic world, author-defined schedule)

Same drifting world, same seeds and same budget (6000) as Track B3; only the learner is new. Everything is a simulation written by one author. Question: attempt 1 (B3) did not adapt measurably better than the B1 learner; why, and can a learner be made to lose measurably less after a change? Measured 2026-11-05 on branch `b3-v2` (built on c7e5d8c3), code commit 6cc82e2a, with

```
cargo run -p kore-self --example measure_b3b --offline --release -- diag              # diagnosis of attempt 1 (tuning seeds)
cargo run -p kore-self --example measure_b3b --offline --release -- breakdown 0 300   # per-cell breakdown after change 0/1/2 (tuning seeds)
cargo run -p kore-self --example measure_b3b --offline --release -- tune quick|m1|m2|combo|m4|told|check
cargo run -p kore-self --example measure_b3b --offline --release -- report with-tuning   # tables below (about 5 min)
cargo run -p kore-self --example measure_b3b --offline --release -- budgets
```

Every setting was chosen on tuning seeds 101..120; the tables are report seeds 1..20 (n = 20 worlds), 95% t-intervals of the mean over worlds, paired by world. About 70 learner settings were tried on the tuning seeds in total (listed below), so a small gain on the tuning seeds is expected by selection alone; the report seeds are the test.

### Why attempt 1 failed (diagnosis, tuning seeds 101..120)

Two yardsticks were added: an **oracle with the skip rule** (the B3 oracle knows the hidden success rates but never skips a menu, so a learner that skips can beat it; B1 was above it in two of the four regimes in B3, so "B1 is within 0.08 of the oracle" did not mean there was nothing to gain), and a **told-what upper bound** (B1 that, at the true time of each change, is given 20 pseudo-attempts at the true success rate of every cell the change concerns: all units cells; all physics and arithmetic cells at the shift; the `fast` cells, cleared first, at the degradation). Neither is a learner.

1. **There is headroom after the changes, but almost none of it is where the attempt-1 detector acted.** Regret of B1 against the oracle + skip in the 300 energy units before the first change: -0.009 [-0.220, +0.201]; in the 300 after the new domain 0.492 [0.269, 0.715], after the shift 0.799 [0.507, 1.092], after the degradation 0.145 [-0.170, 0.459]. Told-what minus B1, whole life: new domain +0.114 (18 of 20 worlds better), shift cells +0.090 (20 of 20), degradation +0.027 (12 of 20), all three +0.264 (19 of 20). The only change in a hidden success rate (the degradation) is worth at most +0.03 over the life; the other two changes are visible in the offers and cost the learner through exploration, which a change detector does not address.
2. **The losses after the new domain and the shift are failed exploration of hard cells whose prior is too optimistic.** The prior of an untried (domain, difficulty, strategy) cell is the domain's (domain, strategy) rate pooled over all difficulties, which is dominated by the easy tasks. In units, `fast` succeeds 0.82 at difficulty 1-2 and 0.00 at 3-5 (hidden truth, mean over worlds; the old domains average 0.47 / 0.25 / 0.36 at 3-5). Pooled over the 20 worlds in the 300 energy after units appears, B1 made 173 `fast` attempts at units difficulty 3-5 with 0 right and 16 `careful` attempts at 4-5 with 0 right; after the shift (physics pays twice as much, so its hard cells become worth trying) 168 `fast` attempts at physics difficulty 3-5 with about 10% right and 60 at arithmetic difficulty 4 with 8% right. With the prior weight PRIOR_K = 4 and the planner's optimism, a cell with a prior near 0.8 needs about 5 failures before the planner leaves it.
3. **The attempt-1 reaction to an alarm made things worse.** Cutting a (domain, strategy) group to 10% of its weight sends its cells back to a stale prior (the strategy-wide rate, still built on the undegraded other domains) with a large uncertainty; the optimistic planner then tries `fast` more: 125.8 attempts at difficulty 1-2 in the 600 energy after the degradation against 116.4 for B1, and regret in the 300 after the degradation 0.383 [0.041, 0.725] against 0.145 for B1. The detector also works per (domain, strategy) although the degradation hits `fast` in every domain at once (12 of the 20 alarms on the tuning seeds were in units, the domain with the least evidence).
4. **Clearing knowledge creates a skip trap.** A "told when" control that clears every `fast` cell at the true time of the degradation fell to 1.112 [0.336, 1.888] reward per energy in the next 300 energy (B1 3.936) with 4298 skipped menus over the 20 worlds (B1 774): cleared cells look expensive and uncertain, the skip rule compares their score with the realized rate, and a skip produces no evidence. So resetting, or forgetting, is dangerous with this planner.
5. **The attempt-1 cold-start gain is an artifact of a threshold.** The bonus applies while a (domain, strategy) group has "less than 1.0 effective attempt". With any discounting (attempt 1 used a half-life of 5000 attempts; the cold-start-only control 1e12), one attempt decays to 0.99999..., so the bonus actually lasts two attempts. With exact counting (half-life 1e300, same bonus) the same arm goes from +0.090 to -0.098 against B1 on the tuning seeds (7 wins, 13 losses). Attempt 1's +0.03 / +0.04 was therefore not evidence for adaptation.
6. **Small planner changes move single worlds by +-0.2 to 0.3.** Attempt 1 against B1 was 10 wins and 10 losses with an interval of +-0.21; any rule that changes the trajectory early has this spread. Effects smaller than about 0.05 are only visible when the change leaves most of the life untouched (as M1 and M2 below do: their stationary runs are identical to B1 in most worlds).
7. **Relative to its own level before the changes, B1 is not clearly better at absorbing changes than the fixed policies.** Excess regret (mean regret in the three post-change windows minus the regret before the first change): tuning seeds B1 0.488, UCB1 0.519, greedy 0.493, random 0.427. A learner explores new options and pays for it; a fixed policy takes the new offers at face value.

### What was tried (one at a time, tuning seeds only)

New mode `adapt_mode: switch` (`being/adapt_b3b.rs`, hooks in `model.rs`); no forgetting, everything replay-exact and logged.
* **M1 windowed switch.** Each (domain, difficulty, strategy) cell keeps its last W outcomes; after each attempt a generalized likelihood ratio (window rate against the older rate, against one rate for all) above a threshold, with at least `min_old` older attempts, REPLACES the cell's evidence by the window (real recent data, so no burst of optimism and no skip trap). Grid W 6/8/12/16 x threshold 3/4/6/8 nats x min_old 8/16 (32 settings): thresholds of 3-4 nats cost 0.02 to 0.065 in the stationary world (0.9 to 3.5 switches per stationary world, all false); 6-8 nats are within +-0.01 of B1. Chosen W 6, 8 nats, min_old 8: +0.004 drifting, +0.000 stationary (0 stationary switches).
* **M2 prior-data conflict.** While a cell holds fewer than `max_n` own attempts, the log-likelihood of its outcomes under the model's prediction is compared with a flat prediction from its own outcomes (Laplace); when the prior loses by more than a threshold, the cell keeps only `keep` of the prior weight PRIOR_K. Grid threshold 1/1.5/2/3 nats x keep 0.1/0.25/0.5 x max_n 8/16 (24 settings): every setting was at or above B1 in the drifting world (+0.001 to +0.013); thresholds of 1-2 nats won in 14-17 of 20 worlds, 3 nats rarely fired. Chosen 1 nat, keep 0.1, max_n 16: +0.013 drifting (16 / 4), -0.004 stationary (13 / 7), post-change windows +0.085 (15 / 5).
* **M3 sibling spread** (after a switch, the same (difficulty, strategy) cells of the other domains test with a lower threshold): factor 0.5 / 0.75 added at most +0.004; not kept.
* **Cold-start bonus in the new mode** (exact threshold, tested with a temporary planner edit that was then reverted): M1+M2 with the bonus -0.070 drifting, -0.161 stationary; not kept (see cause 5).
* **M4 cross-domain prior** ("priors from similar domains"): while a (domain, strategy) group holds fewer than N effective attempts, a cell's prior mean is the mean posterior of the same (difficulty, strategy) cell in the other domains that hold evidence there. Best case first: B1 given the old domains' mean TRUE rates for every units cell at the change: +0.088 (16 / 4). Realistic M4 alone: +0.009 to +0.026 drifting with 9-11 wins of 20; with M1+M2: +0.025 (N infinite) to +0.086 (N 20), but it also moved the stationary result by +0.055 to +0.081 with 10 wins of 20, i.e. it changes the whole early life, not the adaptation. Kept only as a reported variant (N 20).
* Exploration reset on a detected change was not built as a mechanism: cause 3 and 4 show that more optimism or cleared evidence after a change costs reward with this planner.

The B3b learner is M1+M2 (`DEFAULT_SWITCH`: W 6, 8 nats, min_old 8; 1 nat, keep 0.1, max_n 16; no spread, no cross-domain prior, no cold-start bonus).

At budget 600 B3b also gains in the stationary world (+0.046 [+0.028, +0.065], 17 / 0 / 3 on the report seeds). So part of what M2 does is not adaptation to a change but faster learning of any untried hard cell, which matters most early in a life (at 600 the whole life is "early"). At 6000 the stationary gain is +0.003, so there the gain is concentrated after the changes.

### Verdict

* **B3 is now weakly positive against B1, and only there.** The B3b learner loses less after the changes than B1: +0.095 [+0.043, +0.147] reward per energy over the three post-change windows (better in 16 of 20 worlds), excess regret 0.105 lower [+0.049, +0.160], competence in the new domain about 40 energy units sooner (paired -42 [-79, -5] over the 11 worlds where both get there). Over the whole life that is +0.027 [+0.010, +0.044] (18 of 20 worlds), about 0.7%, and the stationary world is unchanged (+0.003 [-0.001, +0.008]). The tuning seeds show the same signs and sizes (+0.087 post-change, +0.022 whole life). Small, but the interval excludes 0 on the report seeds. Part of the mechanism is generic (see the stationary gain at budget 600): it speeds up learning of any untried hard cell, and the changes in this world are exactly what creates many such cells mid-life.
* Almost all of it comes from M2 (prior conflict: stop exploring a cell whose outcomes contradict the prior). M1 (the change detector proper) flags the degradation in 15 of 20 worlds, faster than attempt 1, with no false switch, but adds nothing measurable (-0.002 whole life alone; +0.007 on top of M2). This matches the diagnosis: the hidden change is worth at most +0.03 over the life even when told; what costs after a change is exploration.
* **Against attempt 1** the whole-life difference is not established (-0.003 [-0.208, +0.201]): attempt 1's spread over worlds is large (cause 6). Its excess regret is larger than B3b's (+0.217 [+0.085, +0.349]).
* **Against the fixed policies** B3b is far ahead in absolute terms (+1.97 against UCB1). In excess regret (loss caused by the changes, relative to the policy's own level before them) B3b loses less than UCB1, greedy and random on the report seeds (+0.29, +0.28, +0.31, all intervals above 0), but on the tuning seeds the same comparisons are +0.13, +0.10, +0.03 with intervals including 0. So "adapts faster than the fixed policies" is not established; B1 itself is not clearly better than them on this measure (+0.19 [-0.01, +0.39] report, +0.03 tuning).
* Most of the headroom remains: the told-what bound is +0.522 above B1 in the post-change windows; B3b recovers 0.095 of it (about 18%). The oracle + skip rule is still +0.214 [+0.011, +0.418] above B3b over the whole life.
* The cross-domain prior (M4) gave the largest tuning gain and did not replicate (-0.083 [-0.335, +0.168] on the report seeds); it is reported, not recommended.

### Caveats

* One author wrote the world, the schedule, the learners, the diagnosis and the yardsticks. The diagnosis was done on the tuning seeds and the mechanisms were designed after looking at it (M2 targets exactly the failure seen in the per-cell breakdown), so the world was in effect used twice: once to see the failure, once (other seeds) to test the fix.
* About 70 settings on 20 tuning worlds; the chosen one is the best on the post-change metric there. The report-seed effect (+0.095) is close to the tuning one (+0.087), which argues against pure selection, but n = 20 worlds.
* The skip-aware oracle uses the planner's skip rule with the hidden success rates; it is a better yardstick than the B3 oracle, not an optimal policy (the told-what bound beats it in some windows).
* The told-what bound and the "told when" control use hidden truth and exist only in the measurement (`measure_b3b.rs`); no learner or tool can switch them on. The cold-start-in-switch-mode numbers came from a temporary planner edit that was reverted; they are not reproducible from this commit.
* Prior conflicts cut a cell's prior weight for good (no restoring); in a longer life or a world where hard cells improve this could cost. A world in which the hidden change is expensive (where a detector should matter) was not built; this world was kept so that the comparison with B3 is on the same worlds.
* Not shown: real data, a real thinker, other worlds, other budgets beyond the line above, long unattended runs.

### What is tested (not measured)

`being/adapt_b3b.rs` and `being/tests_b3b.rs`, `being_tools_b3b_tests.rs`: the switch fires on a window that disagrees with long evidence and not on a steady cell; the prior is rejected after surprising failures and kept when it fits; a switched cell holds only its window; after three failures in an untried hard cell B3b believes much less than B1; switch mode with both mechanisms off equals B1 bit for bit; a logged B3b run is deterministic, every decision is re-derived from the log, the refolded model and changes equal the live ones, every change is a note plus a `belief` revision (author `rule:being-detector`, tags `change_kind` and `difficulty`) citing the outcome events of its (domain, strategy); a run split over two calls equals one run; `adapt_mode` needs `adapt`, accepts only full or switch and is fixed once the being exists (`adapt: true` alone is still the B3 learner); the KILL switch is checked before every step (12 steps when it turns on at the 13th check) and the energy cap stops the run with a logged refusal; through the tool, a missing controller.txt fails closed and is audited, the step cap cuts the run and is audited, a KILL file refuses the run and is audited; the B3b sources name no hidden world parameter and use no file or network API; floors on report seeds 1..4 (whole life and post-change mean above -0.05, stationary above -0.03, the degradation flagged by a cell switch in at least 2 of 4 worlds; measured -0.009, +0.013, +0.001, 4 of 4).

## Track B8: planning ahead (synthetic worlds, author-defined rewards)

Question: does looking several steps ahead with the being's OWN learned model beat the one-step B1 planner (best `listed reward x min(1, p + 1.5 sd) / estimated energy`, skip below the realized rate), and where? Code: `kore-self/src/being/lookahead/` (new files; the only edits to existing files are the module line in `being/mod.rs` and one match arm in `controller.rs` that validates the three new keys). Measured with `cargo run -p kore-self --example measure_lookahead --offline --release -- report` (and `-- tune`, `-- cost`), 2026-11-07, branch `plan-ahead` (from ecf5f695). Tuning seeds 101..120, report seeds 1..20; intervals are 95% t-intervals of the mean over 20 worlds; differences are paired on identical worlds (better / worse / tie).

### What was built

* **Planner** (`lookahead/plan.rs`). Depth-limited expectimax over the learned model with sparse sampling of future menus: every affordable (offer, strategy) and skip at the root; at inner nodes the mean over `samples` menus drawn from the last 64 menus the being was shown (same draws for every branch: common random numbers) of the best of the `width` options with the highest myopic surplus `p x reward - rho x energy`, plus skip; leaf value `rho x energy left + token x tau`. `p` and the energy ratio are the existing model's cells (B1 hierarchy; World L adds a context, see below); `rho` is the reward per energy the learned model predicts for the stationary rule "largest `p x reward - rho x energy`" over the remembered menus (Dinkelbach fixed point); `tau` the learned surplus of using a held token. The immediate term at the root keeps the B1 optimism `min(1, p + 1.5 sd)`. Optional simulated learning: each simulated attempt adds one success or failure to the simulated posterior of its cell (Bayes-adaptive), so information gets value. Iterative deepening 1, 2, ... under a hard node cap; when the cap is reached the running depth is dropped and the deepest completed depth is used; if depth 1 does not fit, the B1 planner decides.
* **Two decision modes.** `pure`: take the option with the highest simulated value (depth 1 = the one-step opportunity-cost rule `p x reward - rho x energy`, not the B1 ratio rule). `hybrid`: the B1 score plus `lambda x (Q_depth - Q_1) / energy`, the value the simulated future steps add beyond depth 1, per unit of the option's energy; the B1 skip rule on the result. At depth 1 the hybrid is the B1 planner exactly (tested).
* **Controller** (`controller.txt`, `lookahead/ctl.rs`): `lookahead = on|off` (default off), `max_lookahead_nodes` (default 20000, hard maximum 2000000), `max_lookahead_depth` (default 3, hard maximum 6). Bad values make the whole file unparseable (B5 rule); missing or unparseable file = fail closed (lookahead off, and the World L run itself is refused and the refusal logged). A request the file does not allow, a depth above the cap and the first node-cap cut of a run are `controller_refusal` events in the being's log. Kill switch: checked before every step (`Policy::gate_cost`), stop logged.
* **Evidence.** Every World L decision is a decision event (with the menu it was shown) and a `decision` revision citing the genesis event and the latest outcomes, whose rationale is the plan: every root option with posterior, energy, immediate value, value after success and after failure, `Q` at the depth used and at depth 1, the decision score, depth wanted / done, nodes, `rho`, `tau`, the learned token rule per family, every model cell the search read (pseudo-counts, reads) and the memory steps of the menus it drew. The being's state (model, token, context, menu memory) folds back from its log exactly, also across a resumed run (tested).
* **World L** (`lookahead/worldl.rs`), opt-in, seeded, its own log source `being:worldl`. A menu per step (fixed offers plus 2 or 3 drawn ones), listed cost and reward per family, the three strategies with the usual energy factors, success drawn from a hidden per-(family, strategy) probability with the world's own hash (identical draws for every policy). Settings: `plain` (control: 4 ordinary families); `keys` (a key family, reward 1 for 4 energy, gives a token on success, at most one held; a vault family, reward 18..26 for 4 energy, can be attempted only with a token, which it uses up; ordinary families pay 0.6..1.2 per listed energy; the menu shows which offers need a token, the being is not told which family gives tokens); `probe` (a job, cost 10, reward 20..28, on every menu: `fast` works in hidden phase 0, `careful` in phase 1, `deep` in both at twice the energy, the phase is drawn again after each job attempt; a probe, cost 1, on every menu, succeeds exactly in phase 0); `sizes` (small offers, cost 2..3, 1.5..1.9 per listed energy, drawn half as often as large ones, cost 12..16, 1.3..1.7). The World L model is the B1 model with one more level: cell (family, strategy, context), context = (family, result) of the previous attempt, shrunk to the (family, strategy) group; all World L planners read the same model.
* **Oracles.** `oracle-dp`: knows every hidden probability, the menu distribution and the token and phase rules (not the phase; it sees probe results like the being) and maximizes expected total reward exactly by dynamic programming over (energy left, token, phase belief), every menu enumerated; a test checks it against an independent memoized expectimax. `oracle-one-step`: same knowledge, best expected reward per energy now, never skips. In the first world and World v2 the existing oracles (`oracle`, `oracle-planner`) are used.

### Tuning (seeds 101..120 only)

First grid (pure mode, simulated learning on, World L budget 400; mean over the four settings of planner minus B1): `beta_root` 0 / 0.75 / 1.5 gave -0.13 / +0.03 / +0.15 at depth 3 (without the B1 optimism the probe setting collapses: -0.9); samples 2 or 4 and width 3 or 5 changed little; depth 3 with 1.5, 2, 3 was best (+0.148). The same planner lost on the controls' tuning seeds: first world (budget 600) -0.10 to -0.24, World v2 (12 families, 3000, noise 50, drift 10) -0.05 to -0.35. Probe setting, probe / job: B1 0.000 / 0.983, pure d1 0.080 / 0.914, pure d2 0.055 / 0.936, pure d3 0.007 / 0.986, hybrid d2 0.032 / 0.933, hybrid d3 0.355 / 0.566, oracle DP 0.114 / 0.842.

The node cap (20000) was never reached in any report run (0 cut decisions in every table): depth 3 needs about 3000 to 6000 nodes per step with 2 samples and width 3.

### What the numbers say (verdict)

1. **Where lookahead helps: the unlock setting (`keys`), and only in pure mode.** Pure d2/d3 minus B1: +0.22 [+0.01, +0.44] at budget 400 (12 or 13 of 20 worlds better) and +0.47 [+0.25, +0.68] at 1600 (19 or 20 of 20). The B1 planner never takes the key (energy share 0.8%), the pure planner spends 24% (400) to 39% (1600) of its energy on keys and vaults. But depth 1 already gets most of it (+0.26 at 400, +0.42 at 1600): the gain comes from the leaf value of a held token (`tau`, learned) and the opportunity-cost rule, not from searching deeper; depth 2 or 3 adds +0.04 at 1600 and nothing at 400. The oracle DP is still +0.43 to +0.64 above (it spends about 70% of its energy on keys and vaults): the learned planner discovers the token rule late and does not chain key and vault reliably.
2. **The information setting (`probe`): no gain; deeper is less bad, never better.** Pure d1 -0.21 [-0.41, -0.01], d2 -0.11, d3 +0.00 [-0.18, +0.19] at 400 (similar at 1600). With known parameters planning is worth +0.34 here (oracle DP minus oracle one-step), but the learned planner does not capture it: the probe's value runs through the context cells (job after a successful probe), which are learned only from probes actually made; pure d1 and d2 probe (8% and 6% of energy, the oracle DP 11%) and lose, pure d3 almost stops probing (0.7%) and ties B1. Turning simulated learning on (Bayes-adaptive search, the mechanism meant to value information) did not help on the tuning seeds (+0.17 vs +0.23 at depth 3).
3. **The energy trade-off (`sizes`) and the control (`plain`): within noise.** Differences -0.05 to +0.07, every interval contains 0. With known parameters planning is worth only +0.03 to +0.05 there, so there was little to gain.
4. **Hybrid mode is the safe one, and it gains nothing.** On World L hybrid d2 stays within [-0.19, +0.07] of B1 with intervals that contain 0, but gives up the `keys` gain (+0.02). Hybrid d3 is clearly worse in `probe` (-0.82 [-1.25, -0.39] at 400, -1.03 [-1.43, -0.64] at 1600, worse in 17 and 20 of 20 worlds) and in `plain` at 1600 (-0.045 [-0.085, -0.006]): the added future term per energy makes the probe (energy 1) look far better than it is: hybrid d3 spends 35% of its energy on probes (oracle DP 11%).
5. **Controls (must not get worse): mixed, not established either way.** In the first menu world every variant is below B1 on the mean except pure d2 at budget 3000 (+0.01): pure d2 -0.21 and hybrid d2 -0.08 [-0.19, +0.04] at 600; hybrid d2 -0.03 and hybrid d3 -0.07 [-0.18, +0.05] at 3000, worse in 17 and 19 of 20 worlds; every interval contains 0. In World v2 the means are slightly positive for hybrid d3 (+0.02 to +0.17) and mixed for the others, again all intervals contain 0, and the hybrid variants are worse than B1 in 11 to 15 of 20 worlds in every World v2 condition. So: **the lookahead planner is not shown to keep the existing worlds' results; it loses small amounts in most worlds of the first world and of World v2**, and it is not on by default.
6. **Cost:** a depth-2 decision reads about 200 to 300 simulated evaluations and a depth-3 one 3000 to 6000, against one pass over the menu for B1 (see the cost table).

Read with the limits: World L and its settings were designed by the same author to make lookahead matter, and the B1 planner, the World L model and the lookahead planner were also written by that author; the keys result shows what a token-value leaf does in a world built around tokens, not a general benefit of planning. The oracle DP is exact only for World L (finite state, enumerated menus); in the existing worlds the oracles are the existing references.

### What is tested (not measured)

With lookahead off (or the hybrid at depth 1) every chooser is the existing planner: World v2 decision by decision (labels, decision revisions, events, truth records, rule passes, final state), the logged World v2 run (identical event ids, texts and tags), the first menu world (rewards, costs, skips, strategies, predictions bit for bit), World L greedy; the B1 and World v2 learner rows of the report are the published numbers. Controller keys: validated, default off, bad values make the file unparseable, fail closed when missing or invalid, a disallowed request is a refusal, the node cap is never exceeded and a cut is logged once, the depth cap; the World L run is refused and logged without a controller file, stops on the kill switch before the next step and logs it; plans with evidence are in every decision revision; the state folds back from the log and a resumed run equals one long run; the planner is deterministic; the oracle DP equals an independent memoized expectimax; World L rules (vault needs a token, probe tells the phase, menus pure functions of seed and step); the lookahead sources use no file, network, process or clock API and the planner files name no hidden parameter of any world.

### What B8 does not show

A benefit of planning ahead outside a world built to reward it; that the simulated-learning variant values information usefully (it did not here); that the controls are unharmed (they are not shown to be); any real-world task. No tool exposes the World L being yet (library and measurement only); replay re-derivation of lookahead decisions from the log is not implemented (the state folds back, the decisions are not re-checked).

## Long run (unattended, with restarts; synthetic world, author-defined rewards)

Details, commands and all tables: `docs/longrun.md`. Harness `kore-self/examples/longrun_being.rs`, branch `longrun`,
code of commit c7e5d8c3, 2026-11-05, Windows, 8 CPUs, 34 GB RAM, machine at 98-100% CPU from other work the whole
time (wall times are upper bounds). The real binary is driven over stdio (`being_run`, chooser model, extended2,
discovery every 10 steps, composition and pruning, controller.txt safe defaults), one process per 10,000 steps (a
cold restart each time), log format 3. One world per configuration (n = 1), so there are no intervals.

| quantity | world 1 (no rules found) | world 4 (12 rules) |
|---|---|---|
| steps reached (target 1,000,000) | 390,000 in 3.65 h, 40 restarts; ended by the memory guard | 44,275 in 4.3 h; stopped by hand (0.56 s per step) |
| reward per energy, first window -> last window | 4.095 -> 4.030 (windows of 50,000) | 3.537 -> 3.821 (windows of 5,000; flat at 3.80-3.85 after 5,000 steps) |
| regret vs an oracle that knows the hidden success rates and skips optimally | +0.063 -> +0.128 (rising after 200,000 steps) | +0.367 -> +0.05 to +0.11 |
| repeated known mistakes (attempt on a choice whose own record had >= 10 tries and <= 10% right), per 1000 attempts | 0 in every window | 0.6 in the first window, then 0 |
| wrong answers that came from a rule | none used | 183 of 5,744; all execution slips, the rule's own prediction was right every time |
| `verify()` at checkpoints / replayed decisions / open_at re-checks | 8 of 8 ok / 2,400, 0 mismatches / 4 of 4 identical | 3 of 3 ok / 900, 0 mismatches / - |
| caps exceeded / KILL | none / KILL at 300,000 steps: 0 steps after the file, but the answer took 174 s (log loading) | none (max 12 live rules, 6 blocks) / - |
| log on disk | 611-618 bytes per step, flat (238 MB); format 1 at 50,000 steps: 2,582 bytes per step | 758-760 bytes per step |
| probe commit time | 8-20 ms median, no growth with log size | 10-13 ms |
| restart: child peak memory, time of a 5,000-step call | 136 MB -> 5.2 GB (about 13 KB per step), 17 s -> 446 s: both linear in the history | 161 MB -> 717 MB; 239 s -> 2,787 s per call (discovery and pruning scan all examples) |

Restart invariance: an in-process single run of 20,000 steps gives exactly the same 60,016 being events as the
chunked, KILL-interrupted log. Torn writes on copies (torn journal tail, stray segment, lost last commit, flipped byte):
the first two recover on the next run, the lost commit is redone with identical events, the flipped byte is refused.
**Not shown**: 1,000,000 steps (memory and restart time grow linearly with the history), a real crash during a
commit, speeds on an idle machine, more than one world per configuration, the cause of the slow decline in world 1. (The cause was found later, Track B11: a skip bar that is too strict once the optimism bonus has shrunk; an opt-in fix removes the decline in-process.)

**Restart fix** (branch `restart-fix`, 2026-11-06, same shared machine; details in `docs/longrun.md`, "Restart fix"):
the log's open now streams the non-event tables into the index a chunk at a time, the being folds its state from an
events-only read, `being_run` reads only the genesis before its checks (no load of the history) and opens and folds
the log once per call. No format change. One 5,000-step `being_run` call on cut copies of the 390,000-step log, old ->
new binary:

| steps in the log | process peak MB | call s | KILL file present before the call: s to the refusal |
|---|---|---|---|
| 49,975 | 698 -> 109 | 19.4 -> 12.5 | 8.6 -> 2.9 |
| 149,825 | 2,057 -> 280 | 69.4 -> 21.0 | 44.6 -> 7.5 |
| 249,675 | 3,423 -> 403 | 185.4 -> 30.2 | 162.7 -> 24.9 |
| 390,000 | 5,275 -> 566 | 774.6 -> 39.8 | 248.8 -> 25.4 |

Restart memory is now the log's index, about 1.5 to 2 KB per step; open time still grows linearly (every segment file
is read and hashed). The rows both binaries append from the same cut are identical field by field at all four sizes,
and a 20,000-step smoke run from an empty log is identical (60,016 events, 20,000 revisions). With the fix the world-1
long run **reached 1,000,000 steps** (5.22 h, 101 cold restarts, shared disk-bound machine): child peak 1,573 MB at
1,000,000 steps (old: 5,201 MB at 390,000), 5,000-step call 8 s at 50,000 steps and 45-140 s from 500,000 on;
`verify` ok, the restart's own fold equal to the incremental fold and steps consecutive at all 20 checkpoints, 6,000
replayed decisions 0 mismatches, KILL at 300,000 steps: 0 steps, answered after 72 s (old 174 s). Reward per energy
per window 4.000-4.098 over the whole run, no improvement after the first 50,000 steps.

**Rule scan fix** (branch `rulescan-fix`, 2026-11-06; details in `docs/longrun.md`, section "Rule scan fix"). The world 4
slowdown came from the rule search and the merge check predicting every candidate and rule on every revealed example
again at every pass (in-process, old code: 4.3 ms per step at 2,500 steps, 78.7 ms at 10,000, growing). They now keep
what they computed per (candidate, example) and only scan new examples (`being/discover_scan.rs`); no cap, no window.
Results are bit-identical to the old code: same sha256 over all being events and revisions for world 4 (20,000 steps)
and world 3 (10,000 steps); the same 132,055 being events as the old binary's 44,275-step world 4 log over its first
44,000 steps; byte-identical output of the B2 (`discover`), B5 (`b5`, `b5-prune-wide`), B6 and World v2 report measurements;
11 tests against the old code kept as reference. After the fix, in-process: 0.2 to 1.0 ms per step from 10,000 to
200,000 steps (64,411 examples), not growing with the examples (it moves with the machine's load). The real binary
reached 150,000 steps of world 4 in 0.47 h (5,000-step calls of 6 to 25 s up to 40,000 steps, 90 s at 150,000; old
code 239 s to 2,787 s up to 40,000); what still grows per call is the restart (log fold and memory, bugs 1 and 2, about
15 KB per step), plus one full scan of the examples per new process (31 s at 64,411 examples).
Note (merge of `restart-fix` and `rulescan-fix` on `brain-v3`): the restart growth mentioned here (bugs 1 and 2) is addressed by the Restart fix. The two fixes were measured separately; the combination has been tested (`cargo test`) but not measured in a long run.

## Track B7: using discovered rules (synthetic world, author-defined families)

Everything here is the World v2 simulation (author-defined families, rules, noise, drift and rewards) and the existing learner of the section "World v2". Question: the being discovers correct rules but its reward barely changes (discovery minus no discovery +0.044 small, +0.024 medium, -0.000 large clean). Is that because the planner does not use the rules, and does using them raise reward? Code: `kore-self/src/being/world2/rules_use.rs` and additive, switch-guarded branches in `world2/{engine,learner,solve,measure,replay}.rs`; nothing outside `world2/` changed. Measured with `cargo run -p kore-self --example measure_rules_use --offline --release -- report` (also `-- tune`, `-- ablation`) and the diagnostics `--example diag_rules_use -- report|tune`, 2026-11-06, branch `rules-use` (from ecf5f695), commits 50d16758 and b5c770bc. Tuning seeds 101..120 (used only for the choices below), report seeds 1..20, n = 20 worlds per condition, 95% t-intervals of the mean, paired differences on identical worlds (better/worse/tie). Score: TRUE reward per energy (the checker's verdict). Conditions: the World v2 ones (small 6 families budget 1500, medium 12 / 3000, large 24 / 6000; clean, noisy = feedback noise 100 per mille, drift = 20 changes per 10 000 energy, hard = noise, drift and a rising difficulty curve), all 12 combinations.

### Diagnosis (cause confirmed)

Measured on the existing learner, report seeds (the same lives as the World v2 section), counting every offer of a seq or compose cell for which a live rule existed:

| | small clean | medium clean | medium noisy | large clean |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| offers in a cell with a live rule | 1910 | 3979 | 2488 | 7325 |
| rule applies to the prefix / gives the checker's answer (no slip) | 99.8% / 99.8% | 99.8% / 99.8% | 99.3% / 99.3% | 99.8% / 99.8% |
| careful / deep would be right on the same tasks | 84.7% / 85.8% | 92.2% / 92.2% | 80.9% / 80.9% | 88.9% / 93.0% |
| planner's estimate for `discovered` there (mean) | 0.446 | 0.516 | 0.443 | 0.326 |
| best estimate of the other strategies (mean) | 0.806 | 0.714 | 0.717 | 0.869 |
| `discovered` cell never tried since the rule (share of these offers) | 88% | 76% | 82% | 100% |
| offers taken / taken with `discovered` | 974 / 168 | 2143 / 577 | 1135 / 324 | 3527 / 0 |
| accepted rules in classes `careful` already solves (arithmetic, geometric, quadratic, Fibonacci-like) | 31 of 44 | 59 of 77 | 29 of 54 | 89 of 104 |

So: the rule is right on almost every task it covers, but the planner never learns that. Accepting a rule resets the (family, difficulty, discovered) cell, and the reset cell's prior is the pooled estimate of the `discovered` strategy, which is built from attempts where no rule applied (then `discovered` is `careful` under another name) on every family and type. In the large clean world the 84 `discovered` attempts made before any rule existed left the pooled estimate low (mean 0.33 on the covered offers), and none of the 104 correct rules was ever used. Second finding: most accepted rules (54% to 86%) are for classes that `careful` already answers at the same energy, so even perfect use of them changes little.

### What was changed (each a switch, off by default)

* **A, rule estimate**: when a live rule covers an offer's (base family, difficulty), the planner's estimate for `discovered` on that offer is a Beta posterior with prior mean (S + 1) / (S + M + 2) from the rule's own record (S examples reproduced at acceptance, training plus held out; M examples missed, 0 under the B2 guard) and prior weight min(S + M + 2, rule_k), updated by the reported outcomes of the attempts this rule answered on this (family, difficulty).
* **A2, discovered only where a rule applies**: without a covering rule `discovered` is not offered to the planner (it would be `careful` at the same energy).
* **B, noise-robust acceptance**: a plain grammar form that misses some revealed answers is also accepted if the 95% Wilson lower bound of its share right (where it applies) is at least theta, with B2's support rule (3 new training, 1 new held-out examples); with no miss it is judged exactly as by B2 (a test checks that theta = 0 is the B2 search).
* **C, fitted formula constant**: formula outcomes also log the visible input and the task kind; a pass fits one integer g per family from the revealed answers (candidates implied by single examples, 1..1000, smallest first, same split and guard as a rule); `discovered` then answers with it.
* **G, fitted grid move rule**: the same for grid families with the two candidate move rules (4 or 8 neighbours; breadth-first search under the fitted rule at the listed energy).

Every rule use is logged: the action and outcome carry `rule_used:<id>` and the action `rule_record:support../missed../used../reported_right..`; the decision revision cites the rule's note event and its rationale lists the record behind every rule-based estimate; constants are notes and revisions citing their examples. All uses go through the same step: controller caps (constants count as live rules for `max_live_rules`), energy cap, and the KILL check before every step (tested with the switches on). With every switch off, logs, states and measurements are byte-identical to ecf5f695 (golden digests in `world2/tests_use.rs`).

Tuning (seeds 101..120, medium conditions): rule_k in 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 changed nothing beyond 0.001 (8 kept); theta in 300..800: lower theta accepted more rules under noise (87 at 300 and 400, 80 at 500, 75 at 600, 65 at 800 in medium noisy) with 0 wrong at every value; reward differences between thetas were within 0.03 and inside the noise; 400 chosen.

Wrong = applicable and wrong on at least one of 50 fresh tasks of its signature (constants: of its family) at acceptance. Rule-answer accuracy = true-correct share of the attempts a rule (or constant) answered; it includes execution slips (3% to 10% per family) and, under drift, rules that went stale.

### Original worlds

No file outside `world2/` and the two new examples changed (`git diff --stat ecf5f695` lists nothing else). Rerun on this branch, the original measurements reproduce their recorded numbers exactly: B2 (`measure_being -- discover`, budget 3000, report seeds) discovery minus no discovery +0.162 [+0.000, +0.324] 8/7/5; B5 (`-- b5-compose`) composition minus grammar only +0.006 [-0.008, +0.019] 2/1/17; B6 (`-- b6`) transfer minus no transfer, first 100 steps, +0.211 [+0.054, +0.367] 11/0/9. The B7 switches were not applied to the original worlds.

### Verdict

* **Cause confirmed, fix works mechanically, reward effect of using sequence rules: none measurable.** With A the planner uses the rules (large clean: 0 to 1179 rule answers, 93% right), but A minus the current learner is between -0.057 and +0.023 in every condition, significant only once and negative (large noisy -0.021 [-0.039, -0.003]). With the redundant arm removed, the sequence rules add +0.004 to +0.036 (A+A2 minus no arm); no interval clearly excludes 0 (closest: large noisy +0.004 [+0.000, +0.009]). Reason: most accepted rules duplicate `careful`, and for the rest `deep` (twice the energy) or the being's choice of other families already earns about as much.
* **Robust acceptance (B)** finds more correct rules under noise (up to +50%), 0 wrong of 985, but its reward effect is -0.009 to +0.019, none significant.
* **The largest gain does not come from rules: it comes from removing the `discovered` arm where no rule applies.** That arm is `careful` under another name; the B1 planner explores it separately and in some worlds locks into the careful-like arms instead of `fast`. Without it (no arm): +0.20 to +0.26 in the medium conditions (significant), small and large mostly not. The per-world differences are large in both directions (tuning seeds: +1.06 to -1.38), i.e. this is a change of exploration path more than a steady gain, and it says the B1 planner is sensitive to a redundant option. It is reported as a planner finding, not as rule use.
* **Fitting hidden constants from revealed answers pays.** C (formula g) +0.025 to +0.124, significant in 8 of 12 conditions; G (grid move rule) -0.006 to +0.122, no interval excludes 0; A+C+G +0.020 to +0.267, significant in 8 of 12 (all clean and drift conditions, small and medium noisy), not in the hard conditions or large noisy; 658 constants, 0 wrong.
* **All switches together**: +0.198 to +0.439, better in 12 to 17 of 20 worlds, significant in 11 of 12 conditions (not small hard); share of oracle-knows-rules from 0.75-0.86 to 0.84-0.94. The gap to oracle-knows-rules is about halved, not closed: +0.20 to +0.57 remains (oracle better in 16 to 20 of 20).

### Caveats

The fitted constant and move rule are each one integer chosen from a candidate set the author knows contains the truth (g in 1..1000, move rule 4 or 8); the formula kinds are visible in the task. Rules and constants are never retired, so drift leaves stale ones (up to 25 per 20 large-drift worlds); the A estimate lowers their score through reported failures but nothing removes them. The A2 gain is a property of the B1 planner (pooled priors, a duplicated arm), not of rules, and its size varies strongly per world. The robust guard was tuned and measured only on this world's noise model (independent flips, revealed answers off by 1 to 3); no wrong rule was accepted, which bounds nothing beyond these 240 report lives (0 of 985 rules, 95% upper bound about 0.3%). One author wrote the world, the learner, the switches and the measurement.

### What is tested (not measured)

`world2/tests_use.rs`: with every switch off, two logged runs and three measured lives hash to the digests taken on ecf5f695 (events, revisions with rationale, causes; every TrueRec and RuleCheck field); with all switches on, two logged runs are identical, the unlogged measurement takes the same steps, the state folded from the log equals the live state, the switches are read back from the genesis event, every decision replays and every rule and constant is re-derived from the examples logged before it (also after a continued run), every rule use carries the rule id and its record and its decision cites the rule's note; `max_live_rules` holds with constants counted and refusals are logged, the kill switch stops before the next step, the energy cap stops the run; the robust search at threshold 0 equals the B2 search on 400 random examples and accepts a form with one corrupted example only under the robust guard; the constant search fits g and the grid move rule and rejects inconsistent answers; `rules_use.rs` names no hidden parameter.

## Track B9: experiments (synthetic worlds, author-defined families)

Everything here is a simulation written by one author: the worlds, the families, the 17-form grammar (plus the B5 transforms in the B5 world), the rewards and the learner. "Experiment" means: the being picks an offered sequence task because its revealed answer is expected to tell its own live rule hypotheses apart or give them the support the acceptance rule needs, not because it pays most. Rule acceptance is unchanged (same search, support, held-out split, never-applicable-and-wrong guard). Measured with `cargo run -p kore-self --example measure_experiment --offline --release -- report` (and `-- tune`, `-- report 1 100`), 2026-11-06, branch `experiment`, commit f4bb0f8a (built on ecf5f695). The whole report takes about 75 s. Report seeds 1..20, tuning seeds 101..120. Intervals: 95% t-interval of the mean over 20 worlds; paired differences on identical worlds, wins/losses/ties.

Design (`kore-self/src/being/experiment.rs`, `experiment_menu.rs`, `world2/experiment.rs`). For each signature the being keeps every candidate of the search space that has never been applicable-and-wrong on its revealed examples (the live hypotheses), weight 2^-(size) x 0.5^(examples where it was not applicable). For an offered sequence task it sees the prefix and computes each hypothesis's prediction; the predictions split the hypotheses into groups (predict v / not applicable). Value = expected information gain of the revealed answer in bits (sum_v P(G_v) log2 1/(P(G_v)+P(N)) + P(N) log2 1/P(N)) + the expected share of the missing minimum support (3 training + 1 held-out) it supplies; 0 if the being's own accepted rule already applies to the prefix. The unchanged B1 planner proposes its choice; the experimenter scores (p x reward + kappa x value x reward) / estimated energy per (offered sequence task, strategy) with the planner's own estimates and runs the experiment only if that beats the best exploit option (highest p x reward / energy) and the budget allows it. Controls: random probe = a uniformly random offered sequence task (seeded), best strategy for it, paced to the same budget: either the experimenter's realised energy share in that world (random-matched) or the cap (random-cap). Ablations: split term only, support term only. Oracle-knows-rules as in World v2 / B2 (no rule oracle exists for the B5 world). "Targets": (family, difficulty) signatures of sequence families with an in-grammar rule (World v2), or the hidden families the search space can express (B2: 6, B5: 10). A target counts as covered when an accepted rule is right on at least 90% of fresh tasks (World v2: 50 tasks at acceptance; menu worlds: 100 tasks, as in B2/B5). Wrong rule at acceptance: applicable and wrong on fresh tasks of its signature (World v2: 50 at acceptance; menu worlds: 300). Energy share until covered: energy spent before the target was covered over the life budget, 1 if never, mean over targets.

Tuning (seeds 101..120, World v2 medium clean and B2 budget 3000; objective fixed before the runs: the sum over the two worlds of the paired reward-per-energy difference against passive, ties broken by the energy share): kappa 0.1 / 0.25 / 0.5 / 1 / 2 x budget 50 / 100 / 200 per mille of the life budget. World v2 lost reward in all 15 settings (-0.065 to -0.323; 0.1/50 best), B2 changed by -0.073 to +0.096 (+0.096 [+0.023, +0.169] at 2/50); larger kappa and budget covered more targets (World v2 +1.35 to +10.7 per world). Chosen: kappa 0.25, budget 50 per mille (sum -0.057; 0.1/50 gave -0.059). One wrong rule appeared on the tuning seeds (World v2, kappa 1, budgets 100 and 200), none in any other setting.

### Verdict

* **Rules are learned faster, and more of them**: in 10 of 10 conditions experiments covered more targets than passive discovery on average (interval above 0 in 8) and reached them with less energy (interval below 0 in 9), with 0 wrong rules in every arm. In the B2 world at budget 600 there is no effect (7 experiments per world).
* **Against random probes with the same budget**: in the menu worlds (B2 3000, B5) and the large World v2 conditions the information-gain choice covers clearly more (+1.25 to +2.40 targets); in the small and medium World v2 conditions random probes cover as many (differences -0.25 to +0.35, intervals include 0) but earn less (experiments earn more in 15 to 19 of 20 worlds, significant only in small clean).
* **It does not earn more**: at the tuned setting reward per energy against passive is within [-0.373, +0.296] everywhere, the point estimate is negative in 8 of 10 conditions and significantly negative in the B2 world at budget 600 (-0.144 [-0.282, -0.006]); regret to oracle-knows-rules is not reduced. The extra rules are not turned into reward because the planner barely uses rules (World v2 finding 1; that is the subject of B7) while experiments cost about 5% of the energy. The secondary setting learns far more rules (+8 to +20 targets in medium and large World v2) at no measured reward cost or gain. **Negative result for reward, positive for rule-learning speed.**

### What is tested (not measured)

`kore-self/src/being/tests_b9.rs`, `kore-self/src/being_v2_exp_tools_tests.rs`: the value of information (split, support, resolved signatures, verdict kept/rejected), the incremental hypothesis cache equals a fresh one; the decision obeys kappa, the energy share and the count (zero budget = never); experiments off by default: with a zero budget the experimenter makes exactly the current learner's decisions over whole lives in World v2 and in both menu worlds (identical records and state), plain `run_v2` logs are unchanged and carry no experiment records, the B9 measurement runner reproduces the B2 runner; controller.txt keys `experiments`, `max_experiment_energy_pm`, `max_experiments_per_run` (default off and 0, hard maxima 500 and 5000; bad, repeated or out-of-range values make the file unparseable, fail closed); determinism of two logged runs; replay from the log alone of every experimenter decision (400 of 400), of the learner's own decisions by the existing replay and of every rule; each experiment has a note and a revision citing its decision, outcome and note events with the predicted split and the kept and rejected hypotheses; each rule resting on an experiment's example has a credit revision citing the rule and the experiment notes; budget refusals are `controller_refusal` events; KILL stops an experiment run before the next step (checked before every step) and a KILL file refuses it at the tool; tool: experiments refused and audited unless `experiments = on` with a budget, then logged and replayed in `being_status_v2`; the experiment sources name no hidden world parameter (the core names no world at all).

### What B9 does not show

No reward gain; the hypothesis space, the families, the worlds and the oracle are the author's; experiments only choose among offered tasks (no free probe action exists in these worlds); the split term rarely separates applicable rules (the acceptance guard already makes forms rarely applicable to the same prefix); under feedback noise experiments can reject a right hypothesis because the told answer was wrong; the first world's logged loop does not run experiments (measured in memory with the same engine); 20 worlds per condition, one budget per World v2 size, a tuning grid over two worlds only.

## Track B10: all skills together (synthetic world, author-defined families)

Everything here is the World v2 simulation (author-defined families, rules, noise, drift and rewards) and the being's own learner. Question: with every skill built so far switched on together in World v2 (B7 rule use, B9 experiments, B3b adaptation, B8 lookahead, and a new rule retirement), does the combination beat B7 alone, and do the parts help or get in each other's way? Code: `kore-self/src/being/world2/{all_skills,skills,observe}.rs` (new), additive, switch-guarded hooks in `world2/{engine,model,experiment,measure,replay}.rs` and `lookahead/adapt.rs`, one validation arm in `controller.rs`; tools in `being_v2_tools.rs`. Measured with `cargo run -p kore-self --example measure_all_skills --offline --release -- report-look` (and `-- tune`), 2026-11-07, branch `all-skills` (from 4feb8daf). Tuning seeds 101..120 (only for the two choices below), report seeds 1..20, n = 20 worlds per condition, 95% t-intervals of the mean, paired differences on identical worlds (better/worse/tie). Score: TRUE reward per energy (the checker's verdict). Conditions: the 12 World v2 conditions of Track B7, plus three with strong drift (60 changes per 10 000 energy) for retirement. The report takes about 3 minutes.

### What the profile turns on

One request (`being_run_v2` with `"profile": "all_skills"`, or `all_skills::grant` in code) asks for every part; each part runs only if its own `controller.txt` key allows it, otherwise it stays off and a `controller_refusal` is logged in the being's log and audited (missing or invalid file: everything off, the run itself refused as before):

| part | controller key(s) | what it does in World v2 | fixed when |
|---|---|---|---|
| B7 rule use | `rules_use = on` | switches A (rule-record estimate), A2 (no `discovered` arm without a rule), B (robust acceptance, Wilson bound 0.4), C (fitted formula constant), G (fitted grid move rule), rule prior cap 8: the B7 "all" setting | creation (genesis) |
| B3b adaptation | `adaptation = on` | the B3b mechanisms (M1 windowed switch W 6 / 8 nats / min_old 8, M2 prior conflict 1 nat / keep 0.1 / max_n 16, the tuned `DEFAULT_SWITCH`) on the family-keyed model; every change is a `w2_change` note and a `belief` revision citing the outcomes of its (family, strategy) | creation |
| rule retirement (new) | `rule_retirement = on` | see below | creation |
| B9 experiments | `experiments = on`, `max_experiment_energy_pm`, `max_experiments_per_run` | the B9 experimenter around the B7 learner, kappa 0.1, at most min(50, controller) per mille of the life budget | per run |
| B8 lookahead | `lookahead = on`, `max_lookahead_nodes`, `max_lookahead_depth` | the B8 planner in hybrid mode at depth min(2, cap), over the B7 learner: the tree reads the rule-record estimates, and with A2 a `discovered` option without a rule has success 0 in the tree | per run |

B8 can run in World v2 as built (Track B8 measured it there); it is integrated as the exploit choice inside the experimenter (the experimenter still decides whether an offered sequence task is worth more as an experiment). Lookahead decisions are not re-derived by the replay (as in B8); everything else is.

**Rule retirement.** At every discovery interval (10 steps), before the discovery pass, every live rule (sequence rule or fitted constant) is checked against the revealed answers logged since it was accepted, on the tasks of its signature (family for a constant) where it applies: over the last 6 such answers, if there are at least 4 and the 95% Wilson upper bound of its share right is below 0.5, the rule is retired. The retirement is a `rule_retired` note and a `rule` revision (author `rule:being-retire`) that cites the rule's note and every outcome event it got wrong in the window; the rule is never applied again, the `discovered` cells it served start over, and the examples of its signature logged before the retirement are no longer searched, so a rule for the new regime can be accepted from the answers that follow. Opt-in, fixed at creation, folded back from the log. Revealed answers are what the being was told (with feedback noise a right rule can look wrong on a few; the bound needs most of the window to be wrong).

Tuning (seeds 101..120). Retirement: upper bound 0.3 / 0.4 / 0.5 / 0.6 with window 10 (min 6), and 0.5 with window 6 (min 4) and 16 (min 8), on medium clean, medium drift, medium hard, large drift, medium drift60; objective fixed before the runs: fewest rules stale at the end, then reward. All settings retired only stale rules (0 of 280 retirements, counted per setting, were of a rule still right on >= 90% of fresh tasks) and changed reward by -0.005 to +0.005; window 6 / min 4 / 0.5 left the fewest stale rules (3 / 4 / 14 / 10 against 11 / 12 / 24 / 27 for B7 alone) and was chosen. Experiments on top of B7 (medium conditions and large clean): kappa / budget 0.1 / 50 summed +0.035 over the five conditions, 0.25 / 50 -0.169, 0.25 / 100 -0.268, 1 / 50 -0.253, 1 / 100 -0.451; 0.1 / 50 chosen (B9's own tuning, without B7, had chosen 0.25 / 50).
